title: Arbitration & Conciliation Act
lead: The ==Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996== was envisioned as a bold escape route — offering speed, flexibility and finality. Yet as arbitration increasingly mirrors litigation in cost and complexity, has it remained a true alternative, or ==merely a parallel courtroom cloaked in private robes==? In [[Gayatri Balasamy v. ISG Novasoft (2025)]] the SC upheld a court's power to ==modify== an arbitral award under ss.34 and 37.

items: ==Minimise judicial intervention== — limit courts' supervisory role, expedite resolution
==Promote efficiency and finality== — awards final, binding, enforceable ==as a decree==
==Align with international standards== — based on the ==UNCITRAL Model Law==
==Encourage ADR== as an alternative to slow, expensive, rigid litigation
==Support economic liberalisation== — attract foreign investment with reliable dispute resolution

items.title: Part I — Arbitration
items.kicker: Domestic + international commercial arbitration seated in India
bullets: ==Arbitration agreement must be in writing== — a clause or a separate agreement
==Appointment==: parties agree the procedure; failing which the ==court appoints==
==Jurisdiction==: tribunal rules on its own jurisdiction — ==Kompetenz-Kompetenz==
==Conduct==: not bound by CPC or Evidence Act — flexible, party-driven
Interim relief available from ==both tribunal and courts==
==Award== must be in writing, reasoned and signed — final and binding
==Setting aside== on limited grounds: invalid agreement, lack of notice, ==violation of public policy==
==Enforcement== as a decree of the court

items.title: Parts II–IV
bullets: ==Part II — Foreign Awards==: enforcement under the ==New York and Geneva Conventions==; a ‘foreign award’ is one made in a ==reciprocating territory== under a written agreement — enforceable subject to limited grounds of refusal
==Part III — Conciliation==: voluntary, confidential, resulting in a ==binding settlement agreement==
==Part IV — Supplementary==: miscellaneous, including ==rule-making powers for High Courts==

items.title: Key Sections
bullets: ==s.5==: limits judicial intervention
==s.7==: defines the arbitration agreement
==ss.8 & 11==: mandate referral to arbitration; empower courts to appoint arbitrators
==s.16==: Kompetenz-Kompetenz
==s.34==: grounds for setting aside (public policy, procedural irregularity)
==s.36==: awards enforceable as court decrees
==ss.44–52==: foreign awards under the New York Convention

items.title: 2015 Amendment
bullets: ==Timelines==: 12 months, extendable by 6
==Fast-track procedure==
==Narrowed ‘public policy’== as a ground for setting aside
Strengthened ==confidentiality==
Indian courts may grant ==interim relief for foreign-seated arbitrations==
Incorporated ==IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest== as schedules

items.title: 2019 Amendment & Beyond
bullets: ==Arbitration Council of India (ACI)== to promote institutional arbitration and set standards
==Qualification and accreditation== criteria for arbitrators — criticised for ==excluding foreign-qualified arbitrators==
Streamlined procedures — but ==ACI not fully implemented==
==Commercial Courts Act, 2015== for specialised commercial benches
==NDIAC Act, 2019== — a flagship institution for international and domestic arbitration

head: Case
Holding
rows: ==Part I applies only to India-seated arbitrations==; Indian courts have no jurisdiction over foreign-seated arbitration.
The Chief Justice's power under s.11 is ==judicial, not administrative==.
Expanded ‘public policy’ to include ==‘patent illegality’== — increasing judicial intervention.
[[Shri Lal Mahal v. Progetto Grano Spa (2013)]]
‘Public policy’ in ==enforcement is narrower== than in setting-aside proceedings.
Clarified the ==limited circumstances== for modifying awards: severability, clerical/computational errors, post-award interest.

blocks.text: ==Impact of Gayatri Balasamy==: courts have a ==limited power to modify== under ss.34/37 — ==severability== of invalid parts, correction of ==clerical/computational errors==, and ==post-award interest== not complying with the Act. ==No general power to modify== — but ==Art 142 can still be used==.

items.title: Issues
bullets: ==Judicial intervention==; delays; ==costs==
==Lack of precedent==; confidentiality issues
==Bias and repeat appointments==
Limited judicial review; unfamiliarity with ADR
==Statutory vs contractual arbitration== confusion

items.title: Solutions
bullets: ==Strict adherence to timelines==; judicial training
==Promotion of institutional arbitration==
Legislative clarity and reform
Awareness campaigns; ==confidentiality safeguards==
==Arbitrator accreditation==

blocks.text: The promise of ADR lies not just in statutes, but in reimagining justice itself.
